[('e34d562e-ef12-4c4e-9bc0-7c6ae357c015', '2024-06-20 09:19:23.690415+00:00', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'High', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

You are a security analyst. 
You need to answer a given security question by querying the database.
The logs are stored in a MySQL database, you can use SQL queries to retrieve entries as needed.
Note there are more than 20 tables in the database, so you may need to explore the schema or check example entries to understand the database structure.

Your response should always be a thought-action pair:
Thought: <your reasoning>
Action: <your SQL query>

In Thought, you can analyse and reason about the current situation, 
Action can be one of the following: 
(1) execute[<your query>], which executes the SQL query
(2) submit[<your answer>], which is the final answer to the question

Below are some demonstrations. Note that `Observation` denotes the returned logs from the database.
Many of the returned logs are reduced for brevity (replaced with `...`).

Example 1: 
Question:  
An automated investigation was initiated manually by u141(u141@ash.alpineskihouse.co) on the host `vnevado-win10e`. This investigation aimed to identify and review threat artifacts for potential remediation. As part of this security incident, a suspicious process executed a PowerShell command. Can you identify the account name that was associated with this activity?

Thought: I will start by listing all the tables in the database to understand the structure.

tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'High', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures & bcdedit /set default recoveryenabled no]', 'MDATP', 'Microsoft', '7d47542a-7c5a-4fd4-85f2-640f2bf0927b_1', '37ed1840-2428-9ace-8db4-fc7ceeda30b9', '', '', 'WindowsDefenderAtp', '', '', 'False', '2024-06-20 09:10:49.054537+00:00', '2024-06-20 09:10:51.876113+00:00', '2024-06-20 09:19:23.179872+00:00', '["1. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'High', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures & bcdedit /set default recoveryenabled no]', 'MDATP', 'Microsoft', '7d47542a-7c5a-4fd4-85f2-640f2bf0927b_1', '37ed1840-2428-9ace-8db4-fc7ceeda30b9', '', '', 'WindowsDefenderAtp', '', '', 'False', '2024-06-20 09:10:49.054537+00:00', '2024-06-20 09:10:51.876113+00:00', '2024-06-20 09:19:23.179872+00:00', '["1. group', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'High', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'High', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

[('Manatee Tempest activity group', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'vnevado-win11u.vnevado.alpineskihouse.co', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport'), ("Suspicious 'GenRansom' behavior was detected", "Suspicious 'GenRansom' behavior was detected", 'vnevado-win11u.vnevado.alpineskihouse.co', 'Malware and unwanted software are undesirable applications that perform annoying, disruptive, or harmful actions on affected machines. Some of these undesirable applications can replicate and spread from one machine to another. A malware is considered active if it is found running on the machine or it already has persistence mechanisms in place. Active malware detections are assigned higher severity ratings.

•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

[('e34d562e-ef12-4c4e-9bc0-7c6ae357c015', '2024-06-20 09:00:03.183652+00:00', 'Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)', 'Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)', 'Medium', "Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

You are a security analyst. 
You need to answer a given security question by querying the database.
The logs are stored in a MySQL database, you can use SQL queries to retrieve entries as needed.
Note there are more than 20 tables in the database, so you may need to explore the schema or check example entries to understand the database structure.

Your response should always be a thought-action pair:
Thought: <your reasoning>
Action: <your SQL query>

In Thought, you can analyse and reason about the current situation, 
Action can be one of the following: 
(1) execute[<your query>], which executes the SQL query
(2) submit[<your answer>], which is the final answer to the question

Below are some demonstrations. Note that `Observation` denotes the returned logs from the database.
Many of the returned logs are reduced for brevity (replaced with `...`).

Example 1: 
Question:

Can you identify the account name that was associated with this activity?

Question:  
A recent security incident involved multiple stages and suspicious activities. A Mimikatz credential theft tool was detected on a device at 2024-07-04 22:35:03.797541+00:00. Mimikatz is a tool used to harvest plaintext passwords, password hashes, smartcard PINs, and Kerberos tickets. The attacker might be leveraging this tool to harvest credentials to log into this or other devices on the network by impersonating a valid user. Several command line executions involving `mimikatz.exe` were observed, along with connected mimikatz-related files like `mimidrv.sys`, `mimispool.dll`, and `mimilove.exe`. More information can be found in the Mimikatz tool profile Threat Analytics report and the Actor profile: Storm-0875 Threat Analytics report provided by Microsoft. Can you identify the IP address involved in the malicious credential theft tool execution detected?

Action: execute[SHOW TABLES;]

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'High', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures & bcdedit /set default recoveryenabled no]', 'MDATP', 'Microsoft', '3fcede41-9fdb-4dfb-9fd0-69f1c6fa88bf_1', '8edf196f-fae8-6f94-3acd-93c648e9aa1f', '', '', 'WindowsDefenderAtp', '', '', 'False', '2024-06-20 09:29:38.767268+00:00', '2024-06-20 09:29:41.284899+00:00', '2024-06-20 09:39:59.777330+00:00', '["1. Primary Refresh Token (PRT)', 'Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)', 'Medium', "Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'High', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures & bcdedit /set default recoveryenabled no]', 'MDATP', 'Microsoft', '3fcede41-9fdb-4dfb-9fd0-69f1c6fa88bf_1', '8edf196f-fae8-6f94-3acd-93c648e9aa1f', '', '', 'WindowsDefenderAtp', '', '', 'False', '2024-06-20 09:29:38.767268+00:00', '2024-06-20 09:29:41.284899+00:00', '2024-06-20 09:39:59.777330+00:00', '["1. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

[('e34d562e-ef12-4c4e-9bc0-7c6ae357c015', '2024-06-20 09:19:23.690415+00:00', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'High', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

You are a security analyst. 
You need to answer a given security question by querying the database.
The logs are stored in a MySQL database, you can use SQL queries to retrieve entries as needed.
Note there are more than 20 tables in the database, so you may need to explore the schema or check example entries to understand the database structure.

Your response should always be a thought-action pair:
Thought: <your reasoning>
Action: <your SQL query>

In Thought, you can analyse and reason about the current situation, 
Action can be one of the following: 
(1) execute[<your query>], which executes the SQL query
(2) submit[<your answer>], which is the final answer to the question

There was a detection of unknown malware being active in the environment, which was stopped by Windows Defender but it is recommended to further check the machine for signs of infection. Following that, there were multiple alerts indicating possible attempts to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) which is a key artifact used for Azure AD authentication. Additionally, we observed an alert where system recovery settings were tampered with, indicating that adversaries might be attempting to delete or disable built-in operating system data and recovery services. This could prevent recovery of a corrupted system and denie access to backups and recovery options. Various built-in Windows utilities can be exploited to disable or delete system recovery features, posing a risk to system integrity. What is the name of the account involved in the system recovery setting tampering incident?

Thought: I need to find the account involved in the system recovery setting tampering incident. Let me first explore the database schema to understand what tables are available and how they are structured.

Action: execute[SHOW TABLES;]

Thought: The question mentions a system recovery setting tampering incident. This is likely related to registry events (DeviceRegistryEvents) or process events (DeviceProcessEvents) where utilities like vssadmin, wbadmin, bcdedit, or similar are used. Let me first look at the SecurityAlert table to find the relevant alert, then trace to the account.

Action: execute[SELECT * FROM SecurityAlert WHERE AlertName LIKE '%recovery%' OR AlertName LIKE '%tamper%' OR Description LIKE '%recovery%' LIMIT 20;]

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]

•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]

•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

You are a security analyst. 
You need to answer a given security question by querying the database.
The logs are stored in a MySQL database, you can use SQL queries to retrieve entries as needed.
Note there are more than 20 tables in the database, so you may need to explore the schema or check example entries to understand the database structure.

Your response should always be a thought-action pair:
Thought: <your reasoning>
Action: <your SQL query>

In Thought, you can analyse and reason about the current situation, 
Action can be one of the following: 
(1) execute[<your query>], which executes the SQL query
(2) submit[<your answer>], which is the final answer to the question

Below are some demonstrations. Note that `Observation` denotes the returned logs from the database.
Many of the returned logs are reduced for brevity (replaced with `...`).

A recent security incident involved multiple stages and suspicious activities. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

(2) submit[<your answer>], which is the final answer to the question

('e8726a31-a306-23e1-4284-23403d4bd463', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', ('8844d981-1a9a-d893-aa55-acb124bcb188', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

('3f25b0c7-fcf6-aee6-7790-0b8e5ba10dd7', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', ('e8726a31-a306-23e1-4284-23403d4bd463', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. An active unknown malware was detected, which assigned higher severity ratings due to its active state and potential persistence mechanisms. This malware was running on an unspecified host and included processes involving mimikatz.exe and cmd.exe, indicating credential theft activities. Following this malware detection, a possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was identified, signifying that attackers could be trying to acquire this Azure AD authentication artifact to perform lateral movements or credential theft. Can you identify the AadUserId associated with the possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT)?

You are a security analyst. 
You need to answer a given security question by querying the database.
The logs are stored in a MySQL database, you can use SQL queries to retrieve entries as needed.
Note there are more than 20 tables in the database, so you may need to explore the schema or check example entries to understand the database structure.

Your response should always be a thought-action pair:
Thought: <your reasoning>
Action: <your SQL query>

In Thought, you can analyse and reason about the current situation, 
Action can be one of the following: 
(1) execute[<your query>], which executes the SQL query
(2) submit[<your answer>], which is the final answer to the question

In this investigation, there is a possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) that was detected as part of this incident. This is related to Azure AD authentication security threats. What is the Azure Active Directory (AAD) device ID of the host where the possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected?

Thought: I need to find information about a possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) in the logs. This is related to Azure AD authentication security threats. Let me first explore the database schema to understand what tables are available and how they're structured.

Action: execute[SHOW TABLES;]

[('AADManagedIdentitySignInLogs',), ('AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs',), ('AADProvisioningLogs',), ('AADRiskyUsers',), ('AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs',), ('AADUserRiskEvents',), ('AlertEvidence',), ('AlertInfo',), ('AuditLogs',), ('AzureMetrics',), ('CloudAppEvents',), ('DeviceEvents',), ('DeviceFileCertificateInfo',), ('DeviceFileEvents',), ('DeviceImageLoadEvents',), ('DeviceInfo',), ('DeviceLogonEvents',), ('DeviceNetworkEvents',), ('DeviceNetworkInfo',), ('DeviceProcessEvents',), ('DeviceRegistryEvents',), ('EmailAttachmentInfo',), ('EmailEvents',), ('EmailUrlInfo',), ('Heartbeat',), ('IdentityDirectoryEvents',), ('IdentityLogonEvents',), ('IdentityQueryEvents',), ('MicrosoftAzureBastionAuditLogs',), ('MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs',), ('SecurityAlert',), ('SecurityIncident',), ('SigninLogs',), ('ThreatIntelligenceIndicator',), ('UrlClickEvents',), ('Usage',)]

Thought: The question mentions a "possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)" detected as part of an incident. This sounds like it could be in the SecurityAlert or AlertEvidence tables. Let me search for alerts related to PRT.

Action: execute[SELECT * FROM SecurityAlert WHERE AlertName LIKE '%PRT%' OR AlertName LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%' OR Description LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%' OR Description LIKE '%PRT%' LIMIT 10;]

A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?
